---
title: "Student Lecture"
---

Once this semester you teach the class for 20 minutes, on something we do not
cover.

## Rules

- 15 to 20 minutes, one time, on your own.
- 10 points of your final grade.
- The class has to **do** something while you are up there. A talk alone does not pass.
- Pick one topic from the pools below. One student per topic.
- Say which one you want on Discord in `#network-science`. First to ask gets it.
- Your date is set when you pick your topic.
- Show me a one page plan at office hours, one week before your date.
- You can bring your own topic instead. Check it is nowhere in the course, and tell me what the class will do.

## What "do something" means

Good:

- everyone fills in a worksheet
- everyone works a small example by hand
- everyone writes down a guess before you show the answer
- everyone plays a short game
- you write code live and the class tells you what to try

Not enough:

- "any questions?"
- a poll that changes nothing
- a demo the class watches
- a quiz at the end

Ask yourself: if the class had stayed home, would your 20 minutes look the same?
If yes, the activity is decoration.

## Topic pools

Thirty-five topics. None of them appear anywhere else in the course.

### A. Other kinds of network

**SL-01 Two kinds of dot in one picture**<br>
Actors and films make a table. Turn it into a network of actors alone. What did you lose?<br>
*In class:* build the actor network by hand from a small table, and find the triangles that came from nowhere. *Read:* Newman, *Networks*.

**SL-02 Friend links and enemy links**<br>
Is "the enemy of my enemy is my friend" true?<br>
*In class:* mark every link of a small network friend or enemy, find the triangles that feel wrong, and repair them with the fewest changes. *Read:* Cartwright and Harary 1956. Leskovec et al., CHI 2010.

**SL-03 Groups of three, not three pairs**<br>
Three people in one room had one meeting. Draw three separate links and something is gone. What?<br>
*In class:* write a list of three author papers both ways, and find a question only one way can answer. *Read:* Battiston et al., Physics Reports 2020.

**SL-04 The same people on five platforms**<br>
The same people email, chat, and have coffee. What happens if you squash all three into one network?<br>
*In class:* rank six people by number of links in each network, then in the squashed one, and find the person who disappears. *Read:* Kivela et al., Journal of Complex Networks 2014.

**SL-05 Two networks that need each other**<br>
The power grid needs the internet, and the internet needs power. One failure hits both.<br>
*In class:* draw two small networks with links between them, remove one dot, and follow the damage back and forth until it stops. *Read:* Buldyrev et al., Nature 2010.

### B. Things that spread

The network holds still and something moves across it.

**SL-06 When does an outbreak take off**<br>
How catching does a disease have to be before it reaches everybody? A few very popular people change the answer.<br>
*In class:* roll dice to spread an infection on a ten dot network, once on a plain ring, then again after adding one popular dot. *Read:* Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani, PRL 2001.

**SL-07 Some things need more than one friend**<br>
A rumour spreads from one friend. Quitting smoking takes several. What changes?<br>
*In class:* run both rules on the same ring of people, and watch the long distance links stop helping. *Read:* Centola and Macy, AJS 2007.

**SL-08 One small shock brings the house down**<br>
Two identical small shocks. One does nothing. The other takes out everything.<br>
*In class:* everyone holds a card with a number on it, and the class runs the collapse twice from two different starting people. *Read:* Watts, PNAS 2002.

**SL-09 Copy whoever is next to you**<br>
Everyone copies a random neighbour, forever. Where does the network end up?<br>
*In class:* coloured cards, five rounds of copy a neighbour, timed on a line and on a group where everyone knows everyone. *Read:* Castellano, Fortunato and Loreto, Reviews of Modern Physics 2009.

**SL-10 Clapping in time**<br>
Fireflies, power grids and audiences all fall into step. Which shapes make that easy?<br>
*In class:* the class claps, first listening to everyone, then listening to two neighbours only. Time both. *Read:* Arenas et al., Physics Reports 2008.

**SL-11 Why being nice survives**<br>
In a simple game, cheating always wins. Put the players on a network and it stops winning.<br>
*In class:* play three rounds on a five by five paper grid, copying whichever neighbour did best. *Read:* Nowak and May, Nature 1992.

### C. Networks that change

Now the links themselves move.

**SL-12 Timing decides who can reach whom**<br>
The route exists on the map. The meetings happened in the wrong order. Can anything travel?<br>
*In class:* a list of meetings with times, and the class works out who could have passed a message to whom. *Read:* Holme and Saramaki, Physics Reports 2012.

**SL-13 Growing networks get denser**<br>
Everybody assumes a growing network keeps the same number of links per person. Measurements disagree.<br>
*In class:* three snapshots of a growing network, plot links against people, read the slope off the paper. *Read:* Leskovec, Kleinberg and Faloutsos, KDD 2005.

**SL-14 First one in does not always win**<br>
The oldest page should collect the most links. Google arrived late and won anyway.<br>
*In class:* grow two networks side by side on the board, six steps each, and see who ends up biggest. *Read:* Bianconi and Barabasi, EPL 2001.

**SL-15 Dropping the people you disagree with**<br>
People copy their neighbours, and they also walk away from them. What does walking away change?<br>
*In class:* run the copying game again, and let anyone who disagrees cut the link and join somewhere else. *Read:* Holme and Newman, PRE 2006.

### D. Steering a network

**SL-16 Which dots do you have to grab**<br>
You can push on a few dots. How few, and which ones, before you can move the whole system?<br>
*In class:* pair up the arrows of a small network by hand. The leftover dots are the ones you grab. *Read:* Liu, Slotine and Barabasi, Nature 2011.

**SL-17 Where do the sensors go**<br>
You cannot measure everything. Which few dots tell you the state of all the others?<br>
*In class:* place two sensors on a drawn network, shade every dot you can then work out, and try to beat it. *Read:* Liu, Slotine and Barabasi, PNAS 2013.

### E. Structure beyond groups

**SL-18 Small shapes that keep repeating**<br>
Some three dot patterns show up far more often than chance allows. What does that tell you?<br>
*In class:* count every three dot pattern in a small network by hand, then in a shuffled copy of it. *Read:* Milo et al., Science 2002.

**SL-19 Fitting a model when you have one network**<br>
Statistics usually wants many samples. You have one network. How do you fit a model anyway?<br>
*In class:* the class proposes features of a small friendship network, then argues about which set would be enough to rebuild it. *Read:* Robins et al., Social Networks 2007.

**SL-20 A crowded middle and a thin rim**<br>
Some networks have no groups at all. They have a busy centre and a loose edge.<br>
*In class:* reorder the rows of a shuffled grid by hand until the centre appears. *Read:* Borgatti and Everett, Social Networks 2000.

**SL-21 Same number of friends, different job**<br>
Two people have the same number of friends inside the same group. Are they doing the same job?<br>
*In class:* work out two numbers for six people, and place each one on a map of roles. *Read:* Guimera and Amaral, Nature 2005.

**SL-22 When groups cannot be found at all**<br>
Below a certain contrast, every method fails. Not a hard puzzle. Impossible.<br>
*In class:* split two networks on paper, one above the line and one below, and find out which was which. *Read:* Decelle et al., PRL 2011.

**SL-23 Finding a short path with no map**<br>
Short paths exist. Milgram's letters had to find them without seeing the network. How?<br>
*In class:* pass a message across a printed grid, always to whoever looks closest, and count the steps. *Read:* Kleinberg, Nature 2000.

### F. Learning on networks

**SL-24 Guessing the missing links**<br>
Two people share four friends. Will they meet? How do you check your guess honestly?<br>
*In class:* hide three links, rank the candidates by shared friends, and see what the hiding hid. *Read:* Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg, JASIST 2007.

**SL-25 Links that carry a meaning**<br>
"Paris is in France" and "Paris is bigger than Lyon" are two different links. What changes?<br>
*In class:* do the arithmetic for three facts by hand, and predict a fourth. *Read:* Bordes et al., NeurIPS 2013.

**SL-26 Squeezing a network through one link**<br>
Deep models on networks fail for a reason nobody mentions. Information gets crushed at narrow points.<br>
*In class:* count how many dots get squeezed through one bridge at two, three, and four steps out. *Read:* Alon and Yahav, ICLR 2021.

**SL-27 Why did the model say that**<br>
A model flags an account as fraud. Which links made it say so?<br>
*In class:* guess the small piece of network responsible, then delete links and redo the sums by hand. *Read:* Ying et al., NeurIPS 2019.

### G. Drawing a network

**SL-28 What a spring layout is really doing**<br>
Pretend every link is a spring and let go. What does a short line in the finished picture mean?<br>
*In class:* everyone draws the same twelve links by hand in sixty seconds, then compare a dozen drawings of one network. *Read:* Fruchterman and Reingold, 1991.

**SL-29 When the picture becomes a hairball**<br>
A few thousand links, and the drawing answers nothing. What do you draw instead?<br>
*In class:* the same network drawn two ways, one question each, and report which one you could answer. *Read:* Holten, IEEE TVCG 2006.

**SL-30 Dots and lines, or a grid of squares**<br>
Some questions are easy on a grid and hard on dots and lines. Which are which?<br>
*In class:* time the class on "are these two connected" and on "find the busiest group", using both pictures. *Read:* Ghoniem, Fekete and Castagliola, InfoVis 2004.

### H. Networks and people

**SL-31 Networks built from numbers that move together**<br>
Brain data has no links in it. People make links by seeing which signals rise and fall together. What does that invent?<br>
*In class:* compare four short strings of numbers by hand, draw the links two different ways, and watch the shape change. *Read:* Zalesky, Fornito and Bullmore, NeuroImage 2012.

**SL-32 Which links are real**<br>
Every pair of airports has some traffic. How do you drop the noise and keep the small airports?<br>
*In class:* cut one network two ways, and compare what survives at a quiet airport. *Read:* Serrano, Boguna and Vespignani, PNAS 2009.

**SL-33 Names removed is still not anonymous**<br>
Take the names off a social network. Why can people still be found?<br>
*In class:* an unnamed network plus one named piece, and the class puts the names back using link patterns alone. *Read:* Narayanan and Shmatikov, IEEE S&P 2009.

**SL-34 Who gets recommended**<br>
"People you may know" suggests the popular. What does that do to a small group over years?<br>
*In class:* run three rounds of suggest the most connected on a small mixed network, and watch the gap open. *Read:* Karimi et al., Scientific Reports 2018.

**SL-35 Why lies travel faster**<br>
True and false stories move through the same network at different speeds. Why?<br>
*In class:* look at six spreading patterns, guess which ones came from true stories, then see the answer. *Read:* Vosoughi, Roy and Aral, Science 2018.
